I can think of systems that are more equitable. For example, lets say you bring in a game in excellent condition that sells for $60 new. The store gives you a choice.

option 1: you can sell it on consignment where the game has a month to sell before it is returned to you. The store sells it at 10% less than it's present market value new. If it sells, the game owner takes 90% of its sale value. This means a game worth $60 new sells for $54, and the game owner gets $48.60 while the store makes $5.40. The person purchasing the game saves $6. The game owner is paid 2 working days after the transaction is complete to allow for a brief return policy.

option 2: the store buys the game outright at 70% of it's present value new. This would be because purchasing stock becomes a risk. So, on a game that is $60 new, the game owner gets $42 cash. The store sells the game at 10% less than it's present market value, which is $54. The store makes $12 should the game sell before it devalues. The game owner is paid right away.

Even in the case where the store takes all the risk, it's still a better deal for the customer than what gamestop offers. You could offer the very same deal on the consoles and peripherals too. There are a few more edge cases to work out, but a viable model isn't too hard to come by. Right now, gamestop is basically giving you less than 50% of the value of the game new, and selling it at close to full price if it's a recent title.

Yeah, the problem with option 1 I addressed in my comment: people want money now. Chances are if someone is trading in a game it's to trade it for another game or at least money towards another game. Or they need the money for something else. In these cases consignment is not an option for the majority of people, and probably the large majority of console gamers especially. I'm guessing that the reason they don't offer something like this is because the projected increase of profits that might result from that would not make it viable in the long term and would not cover the costs of implementing and maintaining a system for tracking and distributing consignment payments and inventory.

Option 2 would likely run into the similar issues. Not many games sell for their current market value which is why they offer so little for trade ins. It's not just games that are this way, just about anything in the used market is this way. I don't know enough to say that it's impossible to be viable with a model like that, banking on making at best a 20% profit margin, at worst taking a loss of 88-97% (based on having seen bins and bins of used games at several GameStops that sell for $1-5). But it stands to reason that the majority of games traded in are ones that are the least desirable or have updated versions. It's likely these games won't sell until they drop significantly in price.

You have to keep in mind that often times even a 5% mark up may not be enough to break even. There's more cost to running a retail store than just the cost of buying and selling product. You need additional money for the cost of the property (rental fees, taxes, utilities, maintenance, etc), you have the cost of the employees (hourly wages, health insurance, other benefits), worker's comp insurance, liability insurance, advertising, maybe expanding some day and opening new stores, etc. The list goes on. When you start figuring everything out, $12 a game at absolute best probably doesn't cover everything, and now your dream store that was being so nice to the consumers drove themselves out of business.

Gamestop wanting around a 50% return on investment for buying and selling isn't really that absurd. They can't realistically pay top dollar for pre-owned gaming systems, usually when one comes in there are other returns on the way, and every console added back into the market increases availability=decreases value of other pre-owned consoles. If you feel like you can get more from your console no one forces you to take it to Gamestop, find a buyer on your own.
